sense: do good to, be good for
also: it does a lot of good

terms.gloss: do good, benefit, be of use (to)
terms.grammar: verb, irregular (prō + sum), with the dative
evidence: Hor. Ars 333: aut prōdesse volunt aut dēlectāre poētae
Plin. Ep. 7.21.3: balineum assūmō quia prōdest
Traupman 97: prōderit (multum, nihil) tibi, it will do you (a lot of, no) good
Cic. Tusc. 4.30.64: multum prōdest ea quae metuuntur ipsa contemnere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The person helped goes in the dative: tibi prōderit, it will do you good. Lewis & Short: of medicines, “to be good, be beneficial”. The opposite is obesse or nocēre.

terms.gloss: be to someone’s advantage; cui bonō? who benefits?
terms.grammar: phrase: the dative bonō with the dative of the person
evidence: Cic. Rosc. Am. 84: quaerere solēbat ‘cui bonō’ fuisset
Cic. Rosc. Am. 13: quibus occīdī patrem Sex. Roscī bonō fuit
terms.comment: Lucius Cassius’s question in court, cui bonō fuisset?, “who stood to gain?”, which Cicero quotes again at Phil. 2.35, illud Cassiānum.

terms.grammar: phrase: the dative ūsuī with the dative of the person
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.1.3: fuit et mihi et Quīntō frātrī magnō ūsuī
Caes. BG 1.50: utrum proelium committī ex ūsū esset necne
terms.comment: Also ex ūsū esse, to be of advantage (Caesar).

terms.gloss: benefit from, get the good of
terms.grammar: phrase: ex with the ablative of the thing one benefits from
evidence: Cic. Fam. 1.9.20: cum sē maximum frūctum cēpisse dīcerent ex lībertāte meā
Traupman 269: derive great advantage from, multum commodum ex aliquā rē capere
terms.comment: Frūctus is the produce of a field, and so the return one has from anything (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: aut prōdesse volunt aut dēlectāre poētae
phrases.english: poets aim either to do good or to give pleasure

phrases.latin: Balineum assūmō quia prōdest, vīnum quia nōn nocet, parcissimē tamen.
phrases.english: I take a bath because it does me good, and wine because it does no harm, though very sparingly.

phrases.latin: L. Cassius … identidem in causīs quaerere solēbat ‘cui bonō’ fuisset
phrases.english: Lucius Cassius used to ask again and again in his cases ‘who benefited?’

phrases.latin: quī ipse sibi sapiēns prōdesse nōn quit, nēquīquam sapit
phrases.english: a wise man who cannot do himself any good is wise in vain

sources: Lewis & Short: prosum · Lewis & Short: bonus · Lewis & Short: usus · Lewis & Short: fructus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 97, 99, 269, 305, 322.

Horace, Ars poetica, Pliny, Epistulae 7, Cicero, Pro Roscio Amerino, Philippics 2 and Att. 1, and Caesar, Bellum Gallicum 1, checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror); Cicero’s letters Ad familiares against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
